text:
alex: Heads up — saw sustained memory growth on a long streaming session with nested tool loops. KV residency keeps increasing even after tool outputs finish.

alex: repro: 2h conversation, intermittent tool calls, QPS low. heap grows ~120MB/hour, no OOM but unhealthy.

alex: attaching quick heap diff from runtime profiler: ```
# top allocations by kind
kv_entries: 42MB -> 220MB (+178MB)
other_buffers: 30MB -> 38MB (+8MB)
alloc_meta: 12MB -> 18MB (+6MB)
```

maria: ugh. did you try forcing KV eviction manually? like truncating LRU?

alex: yes — called kv.evict_prefix(session_id) mid-run, freed ~30MB immediately but growth resumed.

jiho: can you paste the KV metrics around that time? hits/evicts/residency counts?

alex: ```
kv.metrics: { hits: 1.2k, misses: 430, live_entries: 48k, evictions: 120 }
kv.residency_age_p50: 7m, p95: 2h
```

sam: residency_age p95 2h seems like stale entries. are we keeping tool outputs keyed by exact prompt? tool loop might generate unique keys each turn.

alex: exactly — tool returns include transient traces and a per-request nonce. keys are large (avg 300B). suspect fragmentation and sticky references from the encoder cache.

lisa: do we dedupe keys? we have prefix normalization but not deep canonicalization for tool outputs.

alex: I instrumented kernel selection path — nothing suspicious there. but KV write path shows many small allocations per key (meta + buffer) that don't get coalesced.

ops-bot: deploy 1994032400 -> rolled out patch: debug-kv-metrics (no restart)

maria: can you run a small experiment: strip non-essential fields from tool outputs before storing? see if residency drops.

alex: tried that in a staging run: removing "trace" fields reduced growth rate by ~60%. but still gradual increase.

dan: could this be a profiling blind spot? maybe the allocator keeps freed slabs for reuse and the profiler attributes to kv_entries. check runtime slab reuse metrics.

jiho: also check GC compaction intervals. long-lived goroutines holding references could pin pages.

alex: ran a full heap snapshot and looked at backrefs — there's a recurring reference chain: session -> stream_ctx -> last_tool_results -> kv_entry -> buffer. But the interesting bit: last_tool_results is set to nil after each call, yet backref stays.

sam: sounds like we may be storing a pointer into a pooled buffer that gets re-referenced by a KV wrapper object. maybe shallow copy instead of deep copy.

alex: code pointer: in tool loop we do: kv.set(key, &ToolResult{ data: b[:n] }) where b is pooled. suspect we wrote pointer to pooled slice header.

lisa: yep that pattern will hold onto the underlying array until pool returns it. need to copy bytes or use immutable buffers.

alex: patched to copy: kv.set(key, &ToolResult{ data: append([]byte(nil), b[:n]...) }) and did a 6h run — growth flattened, almost no net increase.

maria: nice find. what's the perf hit for copying? any latency regressions?

alex: 1.8% p95 latency bump on tool calls, token throughput unchanged. overall cost tradeoff looks acceptable.

dan: can we instead change pooling semantics: return copy-on-write or ensure pooled buffers are never stored by references? might be lower overhead in aggregate.

sam: also consider normalizing keys to avoid unique-per-turn keys. dedupe will reduce KV pressure.

alex: agree. followups: 1) short-term patch to deep-copy tool payloads before KV.set (rolled to canary). 2) add linter rule to forbid storing pooled buffers into persistent structs. 3) add e2e test with nested tool loops for memory regression.

jiho: add metric for "kv_pooled_refs" that counts references to pool-owned memory from live KV entries. would help detect regressions sooner.

lisa: I'll add linter rule. dan, can you help design the metric?

dan: happy to. also let's audit other places that store slice headers from pools (tokenizer, streaming encoder).

ops-bot: alert suppressed: kv-memory-anomaly (decision: monitor) :eyes:

alex: thanks all. documented repro and patch in PR #5872. leaving the canary running, will post heap diffs tomorrow. :thumbsup:
